title: Unsung women

cards: Mecca, a room within reach of the sanctuary. A woman sits with a book open in front of her. Across from her, men with pens and paper, scholars who traveled to be here.
She reads Bukhari's collection of hadith aloud, line by line, and they copy it down, checking every word against what they hear, so that later they can say: I heard it from her.

Her name is Karima al-Marwaziyya, and it went into the chain by which that book was passed on. Women were in this history the whole way through, often doing the work while someone else got the chapter.

teach.h: NO WORKER'S WORK IS LOST, MALE OR FEMALE.
teach.b: The Qur'an sets the frame. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost." The chronicles might drop a name; the verse says the work isn't dropped.
So pick some back up, four kinds, all names this path has met. First, a founder.

teach.h: A FOUNDER: FATIMA AL-FIHRI IN FEZ.
teach.b: In Fez, tradition says a woman named Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found the mosque that became al-Qarawiyyin, a place of study.

teach.h: A TEACHER AND A POET: KARIMA, NANA ASMA'U.
teach.b: Second, a teacher: Karima, in that room in Mecca, whose reading of Bukhari's collection men traveled to hear. Third, a poet.
In Sokoto, Nana Asma'u wrote poems in several languages to teach the faith, and trained women teachers who carried those lessons to women in villages far from her.

Zubayda, wife of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, whose name tradition gives to the wells and stations of the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, and other women after her who paid for schools, fountains and mosques with their own wealth, their names cut into stone over doors that passersby rarely stop to read.

Founders, teachers, poets, patrons. The history needed them and often forgot to say so. And the lesson isn't only about the past: in any mosque, school or family today, someone is doing work that nobody writes down.

how: Muslim communities remember women such as Khadijah, Aisha and Fatimah from the Prophet's household, and local histories honor women who founded mosques, schools and charitable endowments.

o: a school founded only for women in Fez
women rulers who governed in their own names
women whose work built the history, often uncredited

p: founded the mosque in Fez, tradition says
poems that taught; trained women teachers

s: the Qur'an says no worker's work is lost, male or female
"Lo! I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost."
women in this history only learned; they did not teach men
scholars traveled to hear Bukhari's collection from Karima al-Marwaziyya.
the pilgrim road's wells were paid for by a caliph's treasury, and his name is on the road
the road is remembered by a woman's name: Zubayda.

games.q: you've inherited money in Fez. you could keep it, or build something. what does tradition say Fatima al-Fihri did?
o: used it to found a mosque that became a place of study.
games.why: tradition says she founded the mosque that became al-Qarawiyyin with her inheritance.

practice: Say today's names slowly, one per breath: Zubayda, Fatima, Karima, Asma'u.

Then think of the woman in your own story whose work made something possible and never got the credit, a mother, a teacher, an aunt who taught the prayers, a colleague who did the unseen part, and say her name too, quietly, if you know it.

wordCard.voice: Unsung women. The founders, teachers, poets and patrons whose work built Muslim history, often without the credit. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they were there. The work wasn't lost, even when the name was. Rest well.
